I'm running the 14B in llama.cpp (a version from yesterday), the 8-bit quantization from bartowski, and it looped on variations of the same paragraph for five minutes before running out its turn budget, in response to a pretty simple chat request that other similar-sized models (e.g. Gemma 4 12B) have no trouble with, a web search and data summarization task, sort of the sweet spot for models this size. My experience with most Qwen fine-tunes is they get dumber, but their benchmark results suggest otherwise, so I have to assume it's a llama.cpp incompatibility.

what
to build and what not to build, defining the overall character and vision of the product, looking at each screen and thinking "how does this help my customer do their job".
This, unfortunately, takes time, as one has to restart many times because of ideas that turned out not to be as great as one had initially thought. And it results in software that is called "opinionated", and often does not follow what the "industry" does.

As a living human being, you have biological or cultural desires and particular goals that you want to accomplish while you're alive on this earth.
When you're creating art or even a product, what you create is a result of your particular values and particular tastes and those drive some sort of purpose for whatever it is you're creating. What you're building is, generally, made for the consumption or use by another person (even if indirectly), and we mostly have empathy and want those people to have a good experience with whatever we're creating. When you use good software, you can sense the intent in what was made. The person (or team) combined their particular point of view with that of the goals of the user. About a year ago I wrote something similar about software, "Now might be the best time to learn software development":
https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44299979

stories.title_en: SIGSALY: Churchill's top secret hotline to the president

comments.author: Merrill
comments.text:
A 1983 review of this remarkable system for the Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers (IEEE) attributes no fewer than eight "firsts" to SIGSALY. They are as follows:
1) The first realization of enciphered telephony
2) The first quantized speech transmission
3) The first transmission of speech by Pulse Code Modulation (PCM)
4) The first use of companded PCM
5) The first examples of multilevel Frequency Shift Keying (FSK)
6) The first useful realization of speech bandwidth compression
7) The first use of FSK - FDM (Frequency Shift Keying-Frequency Division Multiplex) as a viable transmission method over a fading medium
8) The first use of a multilevel "eye pattern" to adjust the sampling intervals (a new, and important, instrumentation technique)
From
https://www.jproc.ca/crypto/sigsaly1.html
I think that the relevant patents remained classified until 1975.

comments.author: Animats
comments.text:
Here's the technical description, from NSA.[1]
It was really an awful kludge. Today, you'd think, digitize audio into a bit stream, encrypt bitstream. That's not how it worked. It was somewhat similar to the older A-3 analog scrambler, which split up audio into a number of bands and rearranged them, changing the rearrangement occasionally. In SIGSALY, incoming audio was filtered out into 10 frequency bands.
There was also a dominant pitch detector and a "hiss" detector for unvoiced content.
That created 12 analog signals to encrypt. Those signals were much lower bandwidth than the original speech. The patent seems to indicate that the frequency band signals were merely encoded as above or below a threshold. Not a full A/D, just a 1-bit threshold. As late as 1973, people were still trying vocoder-like technologies, but it became easier to work on audio in the digital domain and that died out.[2]
The keying system changed the key every 20ms. It's not clear from the description whether the digitization of the 12 signals was also one sample for 20ms, but it probably was. If you used the same key bits for more than one analog sample, that would create a vulnerability. It's a one time ke

comments.author: BoppreH
comments.text:
If you're on Python and your problem is too big for a single regex, but too small for a full-blown parser like in the article, I can recommend the built-in re.Scanner[0]. It's a regex-based tokenizer[1] (so no recursive parsing) in the `re` module, that for reasons is completely missing from any official documentation.
You give it a pattern for each token type, and a function to process each match, and you get back a list of processed tokens.
Importantly, it processes the list in one pass and ensures the matches are contiguous, where a naive `re.findall` with capture groups will ignore unmatched characters. You also get a reference to the running scanner, so you can record the location of the match for reporting errors.
import re
# Initialize the scanner.
scanner = re.Scanner([
(r"\d+",   lambda scanner, token: ('COUNT', int(token))),
(r"\w+",   lambda scanner, token: ('ANIMAL', token.removesuffix('s'))),
(r"[,. ]",     None), # None -> skip token.
])
# Scan a sample string.
results, remainder = scanner.scan("45 pigeons, 23 cows, 11 spiders.")
# Ensure we parsed the whole thing.
assert not remainder
print(results)
# [('COUNT', 45),
#  ('ANIMAL', 'pigeon'),
#  ('COUNT', 23),
#  ('AN
